title: Aim for the Heart
author: Adrian Neibauer
summary: Adrian Neibauer weaves memories of his German immigrant grandparents, whose frugal homes and sturdy handmade furniture showed care even in parts no one saw, with Steve Jobs's lesson from his father about finishing the backs of cabinets. He applies that ethic of craftsmanship to teaching, arguing that teachers resent scripted programs and weak high-quality instructional materials because they know living children, not data points, sit before them. Borrowing Annie Dillard's advice from The Writing Life to aim past the wood for the chopping block, he urges teachers to aim through curricula and tests toward students' hearts. Neibauer describes his own commitment to crafting learning experiences with care in the unseen parts as well as the visible ones. He closes with Dillard's answer to what we are here for, propter chorum, for the sake of the choir, followed by a list of related resources.
points: Neibauer's grandparents, shaped by war and emigration, cared for their few possessions with frugal earnestness.
Jobs's father taught him to craft the hidden backs of fences and cabinets properly, a lesson he carried to Apple.
Neibauer argues you cannot teach a child by treating him as a data point or teaching to a test.
Aiming for standardized curricula or AI-generated texts, he says, may raise scores but makes teaching flat and affectless.
He frames teaching as a craft students help shape, citing Dillard's idea that the page teaches you to write.
quotes: Surviving WWII instilled in my grandparents a frugal earnestness in caring for their few possessions.

So when teachers are told to read from prescribed scripts and teach using shoddy HQIMs, they rankle. Teachers know that living, breathing children sit before them, and that to regard them as anything less is insulting and demoralizing.
You cannot teach a child by regarding him as a data point or teaching to a test. You teach a child by teaching all the way through, aiming for their heart.

As a teacher, if you aim for the wooden standardized curricula, the basal textbooks, or the AI-generated texts, you fail to teach the child in front of you. You may raise test scores, but your teaching will feel flat and affectless.
I do not aim for the curriculum. I aim for the children in my classroom. And when I aim for my students, I teach all the way through to their hearts.
Just as Dillard’s blank page teaches her to write, our students teach us how to teach.
I am not an expert teacher (there is much to learn), but I aim for the heart and I teach all the way through.
